title: Replication & Sharding Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on copying data across nodes (leader-follower, multi-leader, read replicas, lag) and splitting it (partitioning, sharding strategies, consistent hashing, hot keys).

chapters.title: Replication and Partitioning Mental Model
points: Replication = same data copied on many nodes (availability, read scale); partitioning = different slices of data on different nodes (write/storage scale)
Real systems combine both: each partition is replicated, so a node holds several partitions' replicas
Replication fixes read throughput and fault tolerance but does NOT fix a dataset or write rate that exceeds one machine
Partitioning fixes size and write throughput but loses cross-partition joins, transactions and global secondary indexes
Interview framing: first ask 'is the bottleneck reads, writes, or data size?' then pick replication, partitioning, or both

chapters.title: Leader-Follower Replication
points: Writes go only to the leader; it ships a replication log (WAL/binlog) to followers that apply it in order
Synchronous follower: write acks after follower confirms (no data loss, but one slow follower blocks writes); async: ack immediately (fast, but acknowledged writes can be lost on leader crash)
Semi-sync: one sync follower plus the rest async, so there is always one up-to-date copy
Failover steps: detect leader dead (timeout) → elect most up-to-date follower → repoint clients → old leader rejoins as follower
Failover hazards: lost async writes, split brain (two leaders), and timeouts set too low causing needless failovers

chapters.title: Read Replicas and Replication Lag
points: Read replicas serve SELECTs only; route writes to the leader and reads to replicas via a proxy or app-level read/write split
Replication lag = delay between a leader commit and its visibility on a follower; async replicas give eventual consistency
Read-your-writes anomaly: user posts, then reads from a lagging replica and sees nothing; fix by reading own recent writes from the leader or pinning to a replica that has caught up
Monotonic-reads anomaly: successive reads hit different replicas and time appears to go backward; fix by pinning a user to one replica
Monitor lag (e.g. Postgres pg_stat_replication replay_lag, MySQL Seconds_Behind_Source) and alert on it; fall back to the leader when lag exceeds a threshold

chapters.title: Multi-Leader Replication
points: Multiple nodes accept writes and replicate to each other; used for multi-datacenter setups, offline-capable clients and collaborative editing
Benefits: local-latency writes in each region and tolerance of a datacenter outage; cost: write conflicts
Conflict arises when two leaders update the same key concurrently; avoid by routing all writes for a given record to one leader
Resolution strategies: last-write-wins (simple, silently drops data), merge values, CRDTs, or custom app logic on read/write

Leader-follower vs multi-leader vs leaderless: single leader = no conflicts but one write bottleneck; multi-leader = regional writes plus conflicts; leaderless (Dynamo-style) = quorum reads/writes with W + R > N

chapters.title: Partitioning, Sharding and Consistent Hashing
points: Range partitioning: contiguous key ranges, efficient range scans, but sequential keys (timestamps) create a hot partition
Hash partitioning: hash(key) mod N spreads load evenly but destroys range queries, and changing N remaps almost every key
Consistent hashing: nodes and keys on a ring, a key belongs to the next node clockwise; adding/removing a node moves only about 1/N of keys; virtual nodes smooth uneven distribution
Directory/lookup sharding: a mapping table sends keys to shards, allowing flexible rebalancing at the cost of a lookup service that must stay available
Hot keys (celebrity user, viral item): hashing cannot split one key; mitigate with key salting (key#0..key#k, fan-in on read), caching, or dedicated shards for the hot key

chapters.title: Replication and Sharding Cheat Sheet
points: Pick: read-heavy → add read replicas; write- or size-bound → shard; multi-region writes → multi-leader or leaderless with conflict handling
Sync = durable but slow; async = fast but can lose acked writes; semi-sync = compromise
Lag fixes: read-your-writes (read own writes from leader), monotonic reads (pin user to a replica)
Shard key rules: high cardinality, even distribution, matches the main query pattern; avoid monotonically increasing keys with range sharding
Never use hash mod N when the node count changes; use consistent hashing with virtual nodes, and handle hot keys with salting or caching
